back: Inputs, outputs and an objective function that guides learning.

front: Why must an ML metric be tied to a business metric?
back: Companies care about revenue, retention or cost saved; ML metrics are proxies whose link to those outcomes must be shown, often by an experiment.

front: The four requirements of an ML system
What does it mean that ML systems fail silently?
back: The code runs without errors while predictions are wrong, so users and operators may not notice.
Latency: time from request to response. Throughput: requests processed per unit time.
$B\cdot1000/t$ queries per second for batch size $B$ taking $t$ ms.

front: Why use percentiles instead of the mean latency?
back: Latency is a distribution; one outlier distorts the mean, while p50/p90/p99 describe typical and worst-case users.
Sort $n$ values and return the one at 1-based rank $\lceil q n/100\rceil$.
Output a category versus a number; either can often be converted to the other by bucketing or thresholding.

front: Why is multilabel harder than multiclass?
back: The number of true labels varies, so turning probabilities into a label set needs a rule, and annotators disagree more.
Train one model per objective and blend scores $\alpha s_1+\beta s_2$ at ranking time, so the trade-off changes without retraining.
Items not dominated by any other item that is at least as good on all objectives and strictly better on one.

front: Three ways an ML system can scale
back: In model complexity, in traffic volume, and in number of models (for example one per customer).
Many stakeholders, inference latency over training speed, shifting data, and fairness/interpretability requirements.
